1.x: Immediately after declaring that Jerusalem’s Temple was left “desolate” (Mt 23:38), Jesus exits the Temple courts for the final time. This action sets the stage for the Olivet Discourse: his landmark sermon on the destruction of Jerusalem and the end of the age. “And Jesus went out, and departed…”: This is more than a physical exit; it is a profound prophetic act. The glory of God (manifested in the person of Jesus, Col 2:9-10) was permanently leaving Herod’s Temple, echoing Ezekiel’s vision of the Shekinah glory departing the first Temple before its destruction by Babylon (Ezekiel 10:18). “..to shew him the buildings of the temple”: The disciples were awe-struck Galileans. Herod’s Temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world, constructed from massive blocks of white marble (some over 40 feet long) and heavily adorned with gold. They were essentially saying: “Master, look at how massive and permanent this place is! How could this ever be left desolate?”

2.x: “See ye not all these things?”: Jesus forces them to look past the physical majesty to see the spiritual reality. “..There shall not be left here one stone upon another..”: This is a shockingly literal prophecy. In 70 AD, the Roman army under Titus besieged and burned Jerusalem. The intense heat melted the gold of the Temple, causing it to run down into the crevices between the massive marble blocks. To retrieve every ounce of gold, Roman soldiers systematically pried apart and overturned every single stone, completely flattening the Temple mount exactly as Jesus said. Most scholars date the book of Matthew later than 70AD because they do not believe that Jesus truly could predict the destruction of the Temple. Whether the book of Matthew was written before 70AD or shortly after, it was still written within the real witnesses’ lifespan to accurately share the order of events without leaving enough time for legendary myths to develop. Compare this to the Quran, which was written in the 600’s by a single person in isolation, trying to contradict all the early witnesses to tell you that Jesus is not the Son of God and he was not crucified. Christianity has the best evidence by far of any other religion in the world. Its witness never comes from a single person, it comes from multiple people telling the same story within the lifespan of Jesus’ actual eye-witnesses: “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deut 19:15 KJV) - the Bible itself satisfies the Law established by God of two or more witnesses, as it’s composed of multiple books written by multiple people. Even Jesus satisfied this Law with God the Father: “It is also written in your law, that the testimony of two men is true. I am one that bear witness of myself, and the Father that sent me beareth witness of me” (Jn 8:17-18 KJV) - there are TWO (not three) witnesses in Jesus: (1) the man Jesus, and (2) the divine Spirit (the Father) that dwelled in Jesus without losing His omnipresence. We see the two witnesses clearly in: “For there is one (heis: singular masculine one) God, and one mediator between God and men, the MAN(not another god, but the image of the invisible God) Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV) . In Jesus there is more than just the Father, there is a human born of a woman: “I and my Father are one (hen: singular neuter form for one as unity between the human and the divine Spirit)” (Jn 10:30 KJV) - the two are one. Humanity was added to the divine Spirit. One God who is Spirit, and one visible image who is an authentic human person with his own human mind, human soul, and human will that acts as the temple of the Holy Spirit (Jn 2:19), who is the Father of the man Jesus (Mt 1:20).

3.x: “..as he sat upon the mount of olives..”: The Mount of Olives sits directly across the Kidron Valley, offering a panoramic, bird’s-eye view of the Temple complex. The disciples mistakenly assumed that the destruction of such an immense structure must mean the end of human history. They ask three questions, which they likely believed were all part of a single, simultaneous event: (1) “When shall these things [the destruction of the Temple] be?”; (2) “What shall be the sign of thy coming(parousia)?”; (3) “And of the end of the world (aion - literally ‘the age’)?”

What does “The Coming” (Parousia) mean? Most people, when they read the “coming of Jesus” or “coming of the Lord” they almost exclusively assume it refers to the Second Coming, the literal, physical return of Jesus at the end of human history. However, in Hebrew prophecy, and the language of the OT, a “coming of the Lord” regularly refers to a historical, spatial visitation of DIVINE JUDGEMENT upon a specific nation, carried out via human agents (like foreign armies). When Jesus’ disciples asked for the sign of his “coming” (parousia), they were thinking in these OT terms: (1) The OT pattern of God “Coming” in Judgement: Throughout the Hebrew Scriptures, God is frequently described as “coming” or “riding on a cloud” to destroy a pagan nation. These were not physical, visible descents of God’s essence, but historical acts of sovereign judgement. For example, in Egypt: "Behold, the LORD rideth upon a swift cloud, and SHALL COME into Egypt: and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence..." (Isaiah 19:1 KJV) - God did not physically appear on a vaporous cloud; He “came” to Egypt by sending the Assyrian army to conquer them. Or Samaria: "For, behold, the LORD COMETH forth out of his place, and WILL COME down, and tread upon the high places of the earth... And all the graven images thereof shall be beaten to pieces..." (Micah 1:3-7 KJV) - this “coming” was physically executed by the invading Assyrian armies in 722BC. (2) The 70 AD Judgement as Christ’s “Coming”: In the context of Mt 24, Jesus uses this identical prophetic imagery. His “coming” to Jerusalem in 70AD was a visitation of covenant judgement upon the generation that rejected and crucified him. He came in power and glory by utilizing the Roman legion (His instrument of wrath) to put an end to the Old Covenant temple system. This localized, historical “coming” vindicated Jesus as the true Prophet and Messiah, proving His words in Mt 23 were absolutely true. (3) The Greek word “paraousia” literally means “presence,” “arrival,” or “official visit.” In the first-century Greco-Roman world, a parousia was a technical term used for the grand, official visit of a king or emperor to a city. When the king arrived, he would reward his loyal subjects and severely punish any rebellious factions. By asking for the sign of His parousia, the disciples were asking: “What will be the sign that You are taking Your royal throne, executing Your kingly judgement on these rebellious leaders, and fully establishing Your New Covenant Kingdom?” While the NT certainly promises a final, physical return of Jesus to judge the living and the dead, much of the “coming” language in Mt 24 (specifically up to v.34) was completely fulfilled historically in the fiery destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD.

4.x: In response to the disciples’ urgent question about when the Temple would fall and what signs would signal His arrival, Jesus begins with a warning. Rather than giving them a precise date, he cautions them not to misread normal historical turbulence as the immediate end. “Take heed that no man deceive you”: The very first words of the Olivet Discourse are a warning against spiritual deception. Jesus knows that periods of intense political and social upheaval are breeding grounds for panic, vulnerability, and religious manipulation.

5.x: “For many shall come in my name..”: First, notice how false preachers would imitate real preachers by coming in the name & authority of Jesus and not in a nameless, vague Trinity. In the decades leading up to 70AD, Judea was boiling with messianic fever. Jewish historian Josephus records that numerous charismatic figures arose, claiming divine commissions to liberate Israel from Rome. “...saying, I am Christ; and shall deceive many”: Figures like Theudas (who promised to part the Jordan River) and an unnamed “Egyptian prophet” (who led thousands into the wilderness promising the walls of Jerusalem would fall (Acts 21:38), led many to their deaths. They did not necessarily use the name “Jesus,” but they claimed the office of the Messiah (“the Anointed Deliverer”).

6.x: “..wars and rumours of wars..”: During the Pax Romana, the Roman Empire seemed incredibly stable, but underneath, regional conflicts were brewing. From 66 to 70 AD, the Roman Empire was rocked by civil war (the “Year of the Four Emperors”) and the brutal Judean revolt. “..see that ye be not troubled… the end is not yet”: Jesus commands a calm, detached perspective. Geopolitical chaos is normal historical noise, not a signal that the world is instantly ending.

7.x: “..famines, and pestilence, and earthquakes..”: Classical history records several major disasters during this exact window. A severe, widespread famine occurred under Emperor Claudius around 46-48 AD (noted in Acts 11:28). Major earthquakes devastated Laodices (60 AD) and Pompeii (62 AD). “in divers places”: means “in various scattered locations.”

8.x: “..the beginning of sorrows”: the Greek word for “sorrows” here is “odin”, which literally means birth pangs. This is a highly specific metaphor. Birth pangs start relatively mild and spaced far apart, but as the delivery of the baby approaches, they rapidly increase in both frequency and intensity. Jesus is saying that these global disturbances are merely the initial, lighter contractions. The actual birth, the catastrophic end of the Old Covenant age, would be far more intense.

These prophecies serve as prophetic telescoping or dual fulfillment. When an OT prophet looked into the future, they saw events much like a person looking at a distant mountain range. From a distance, two distinct mountain peaks appear to be right next to each other, blending into a single horizon. However, once you actually arrive at the first peak, you realize there is a massive valley of time separating it from the second, taller peak behind it. The Near Peak (the shadow) was the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple in 70 AD. The Valley (the Church Age) is the long span of history we are currently in. And The Far Peak (Reality) is the final crisis of human history, the great tribulation, the ultimate persecution of the global Church, and the physical Second Coming of Christ. Jesus deliberately structures his warning so that the local, historical judgement of Jerusalem acts as a physical, real-time “dress rehearsal” for the end of the world. Both, the 70 AD Prototype and the Final Antichrist Archetype are fully represented here: (1) False Messiahs (local deceivers vs the antichrist and false prophets); (2) The Sacrilege (zealots desecrating the Temple & Roman standards planted in the holy place vs the “abomination of desolation” standing in the third Jewish Temple on a global scale) (3) The Flight (Judean believers fleeing to the mountains of Pella to escape the Roman siege vs the global Church fleeing persecution and seeking divine protection); (4) The Judgement (a localized, historical “parousia”, or visitation of wrath, ending the Jewish temple state vs the cosmic, global “parousia” ending the current rebellious age of man). By studying what happened to the early Christians during the siege of Jerusalem (how they had to stay vigilant, avoid false prophets, ignore rumors of wars, and physically escape when they saw the warning signs) the Church of all subsequent generations is given a perfect blueprint for how to endure the final, global persecution before the end of the age.

9.x: “Then shall they deliver you up..”: The word “then” indicates that alongside global wars and earthquakes, active persecution will intensify. The book of Acts records this literal fulfillment as the apostles were routinely arrested, brought before councils, and imprisoned. “..and ye shall be hated of all nations for my name’ sake”: This is a total shift from localized Jewish opposition to global hostility. If anything negative happened to Rome, the Christians were always blamed for refusing their pagan sacrifices. 10.x: “..then shall many be offended..”: The Greek word for “offended” is “skandalizo,” which means to trip over a stumbling block or to fall away from the faith. When the heat of violent persecution rises, fair-weather believers who wanted the blessings of Christ without the cross will abandon their profession. “..and shall betray one another..”: The ultimate horror of persecution is the collapse of community trust. Roman history (such as the writings of Tacitus regarding the Neronian persecution) confirms that arrested Christians were routinely tortured until they gave up the names and hidden meeting locations of their fellow believers.

11.x: “And many false prophets shall rise..”: External pressure is always accompanied by internal doctrinal deception. Wolves in sheep’s clothing will offer comfortable, compromised theological alternatives to help people avoid persecution.

12.x: “..because iniquity shall abound..”: The word for “iniquity” is “anomia” (lawlessness/contempt for God’s holiness). When societal morality completely degrades and the surrounding culture becomes lawless, it exerts a subtle, chilling effect on the church. “..the love of many shall wax cold”: The word for love here is “agape” - the distinct, sacrificial love that belongs exclusively to regenerated believers. Jesus is not talking about the secular world; he is warning that the spiritual fervor, devotion, and holy affection of genuine Christians can freeze over due to the constant pressure of surrounding wickedness.

13.x: “But he that shall endure..”: The Greek word for endure is “hupomeno,” which means to remain under a heavy weight, to hold one’s ground, and to persevere through trials without giving up. “..the same shall be saved”: Salvation is presented here with a clear, conditional clause. It is not merely about how a person starts the race; it is exclusively about who finishes the race.

The doctrine of Unconditional Election (a foundational pillar of classical Calvinism) teaches that before the creation of the world, God sovereignly selected specific individuals for salvation based entirely on His own secret counsel, without any reference to their future choices, faith, or actions. A necessary byproduct of this view is the absolute guarantee that an “elect” person can never genuinely fall away, lose their “agape” love, or fail to make it to heaven. However, Jesus’ direct teaching in Mt 24:9-13 seems to severely contradict this framework, presenting a model of salvation that demands continuous, free-will cooperation and spiritual vigilance: (1) “Agape” can only free IF it was first hot: Jesus explicitly states in v.12 that the agape love of “many” will wax cold. In NT theology, agape is not a human emotion; it is a supernatural fruit produced exclusively by the dwelling presence of the Holy Spirit (Rom 5:5). Unbelievers do not possess agape. Therefore, for this love to grow cold, these individuals must have possessed a genuine, vibrant, and active spiritual relationship with God. The text proves that real believers can allow the surrounding environment of lawlessness (anomia) to choke out the spiritual life. (2) A real warning cannot be a theological sham: If salvation is governed by a system of unconditional election where the elect are mechanically insulated from ever falling away, Christ’s urgent warning in this passage becomes completely hollow. Why tell a group of people to take heed, to endure, and to avoid being offended if their final destiny was unconditionally locked in place before Genesis? Jesus delivers this warning as a genuine alert: the danger of apostasy under intense pressure is real, not theoretical. (3) Salvation is conditional upon perseverance: v.13 sets up a strict conditional prerequisite for final glorification: Final Salvation = Initial Faith + Enduring to the End. Scripture repeatedly frames salvation not as a static, past-tense insurance policy, but as a dynamic race that must be run to completion. Faith saves us because it keeps us swimming, not because we made an internal emotional assent. Paul warns: "Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; CONTINUE in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee" (1 Tim 4:16 KJV). The author of Hebrews writes: "For we are made partakers of Christ, IF we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end;" (Heb 3:14 KJV). Security is found in Christ, not in an unconditional decree. We are perfectly secure as long as we abide in the Vine (Jn 15). However, God does not overpower human free will. If a believer chooses to let down their guard, yields to the pressure of an iniquitous culture, listens to false prophets, and allows their spiritual fire to die out, they will not endure to the end. Salvation is guaranteed to the endurer, which is why the Church must constantly preach holiness, vigilance, and daily prayer rather than resting on the laurels of a past experience.

14.x: “Jesus specifies which message must be carried: the “good news” (euangelion) that God’s royal reign, authority, and saving power have broke into human history through the Messiah. “..shall be preached in all the world..”: The phrase “all the world” uses the Greek word “oikoumene,” which historically meant the “inhabited earth” or the limits of the Roman Empire. In terms of prophetic telescoping and dual fulfillment: (1) First Peak (70 AD Timeline): Remarkably, the Apostles accomplished this within a generation. Paul wrote to the Colossians around 62AD that the Gospel had been “preached to every creature which is under heaven” (Col 1:23; see also Rom 10:18). (2) Far Peak (End Times Timeline): On a global scale, cosmic scale, the final end of human history will not arrive until every ethno-linguistic people group (“all nations”/ethnos) receives a valid presentation of the Gospel. “..for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come”: The Gospel is not preached to force every person to convert, but as a “witness”, giving every culture a clear opportunity to accept or reject the King. Once that testimony is complete, the old age closes.

What is the Gospel that needs to be preached to all the nations of the world? The word “Gospel” means “Good News.” But to preach the Apostolic Gospel, we must define it exactly how the NT defines it. The Gospel is not a generic message of self-help, nor is it a vague statement that “God loves you.” According to Paul, the core structural facts of the Gospel are the Death, Burial, and Resurrection of Jesus Christ for our sins: “Moreover, brethren, I declare unto you the GOSPEL which I preached unto you, which also ye have received, and wherein ye stand; By which also YE ARE SAVED, IF ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain. For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that CHRIST DIED FOR OUR SINS according to the scriptures; And that HE WAS BURIED, and that HE ROSE AGAIN the third day according to the scriptures” (1 Cor 15:1-4 KJV). The three parts are: (1) The Death of Christ: this parallels our Repentance (dying to sin); (2) The Burial of Christ: this parallels Water Baptism (Buried with him in immersion); (3) The Resurrection: Holy Spirit (New Resurrected Life). The Good News is a message that MUST BE OBEYED, not just mentally believed. Faith is acting as if it were true, it is not an internal mental assent: “I will shew thee my faith by my works” (Jm 2:18 KJV). Paul explicitly warns that those who “OBEY NOT THE GOSPEL for our Lord Jesus Christ” will face eternal destruction (2 Thess 1:8). Before Jesus ascended, he gave the Great Commission to his disciples. This commission is recorded in all four Gospels and the book of Acts. To understand the full, multi-dimensional plan of salvation, we must synthesize these accounts into a single, cohesive command: (1) Matthew 28:19: Go to “All Nations,” baptizing them IN THE (singular)NAME of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost; (2) Mark 16:15-16: go to “Every Creature”, and he that believeth and is baptized shall be saved. In HIS NAME will every sign be carried out; (3) Luke 24:47: go to “All Nations, Beginning with Jerusalem” so that REPENTANCE AND REMISSION OF SINS should be preached IN HIS NAME. (4) John 20:22-23: Jesus sends the apostles out with the authority to declare REMISSION/RETAINING OF SINS through the Holy Spirit. (5) Acts 1:8: go to the “Uttermost Part of the Earth”, and ye shall receive POWER after the Holy Spirit is come upon you. The apostles did not begin preaching the Great Commission immediately. Jesus commanded them to wait in Jerusalem until they were filled with supernatural power from on high (Lk 24:49; Acts 1:4). On the Day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit fell, and a massive crowd gathered, convicted to the heart by Peter’s preaching. They cried out to Peter and the rest of the Apostles: “WHAT SHALL WE DO?” (Acts 2:37 KJV). As a holder of the keys of the kingdom (Mt 16:19), Peter stood up and delivered the definitive, practical application of the Great Commission, unlocking the door of the New Covenant for the very first time: "Then Peter said unto them, REPENT, and BE BAPTIZED every one of you IN THE NAME OF JESUS CHRIST FOR THE REMISSION OF SINS, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost" (Acts 2:38, KJV). Peter’s answer perfectly knits together every single thread of Jesus’ commands across the Gospels: (1) Repentance (Fulfilling Lk 24:47): Peter demands a total change of mind, heart, and direction. Repentance is the horizontal death where a person confesses their sins, turns their back on the world, and surrenders their will to God. (2) Water Baptism in the Name of Jesus Christ (Fulfilling Matthew, Mark, and Luke): Luke 24:47 stated that remission of sins must be preached in His name. Peter matches this explicitly: “be baptized in the name of Jesus for the remission of sins.” Matthew 28:19 commanded the Apostles to baptize in the “name”(singular) of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Peter, under the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, knew that “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit” are titles describing the different manifestations of the one true God, but the redemptive NAME of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is JESUS CHRIST, the ONLY NAME given to men under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). Therefore, every single baptism recorded throughout the entire history of the NT Church was executed exclusively IN THE NAME OF JESUS CHRIST (see Acts 8:16; 10:48; 19:5; etc). The Apostles NEVER repeated the titles of Matthew 28:19 as a formula; they obeyed the NAME contained within the titles: “And now why tarriest thou? arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, CALLING on the name of the Lord” (Acts 22:16 KJV). (3) The Gift of the Holy Spirit (Fulfilling John and Acts 1): This is the modern experiencing of Christ’s resurrection power. By receiving the infilling of the Holy Spirit, the believer is supernaturally born again of water and Spirit (Jn 3:5), receiving the vital life needed to endure until the end. This is the timeless “Gospel of the Kingdom” that Jesus declared would shake the world in Mt 24:14. It is an uncompromised, beautiful message of complete transformation that cleanses the sinner, infuses them with divine power, and prepares the global Church to stand strong against any trial or persecution.

15.x: “When ye therefore shall see..”: Jesus addresses this to his immediate disciples. He gives them a visible, concrete sign that they will witness in their lifetime, signaling that it is time to flee the city immediately. “..the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet..”: Jesus points back to the book of Daniel (specifically Daniel 9:27;11:31;12:11). In Hebrew thought, an “abomination” (shiqquts) is a foul, idolatrous thing connected to pagan worship, while “desolation”(shamen) refers to an act of violent ruining, plundering, or making a holy place completely empty and abandoned. “..stand in the holy place..”: The “holy place” refers to the sacred temple complex of Jerusalem, including the surrounding consecrated ground. “..(whoso readeth, let him understand:)”: This parenthetical note was added by Matthew under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit to urge first-century believers reading this Gospel to pay utmost attention. When this specific sign occurs, there is no time for theological debate: it’s time to act.

The phrase “abomination of desolation” was not a new concept to first-century Jews. They had already experienced a catastrophic historical fulfillment of Daniel’s prophecy nearly two centuries earlier, an event recorded in the books of 1 and 2 Maccabees (I’m not saying that these books are God-breathed or inspired by God; I’m simply saying that they contain true history in them. 1 Maccabees reads as a historical document, while 2 Maccabees contradicts the same story told in 1 Maccabees & reads like a superhero comic book, where the author himself tells you in his preface and epilogue that he embellished the story to satisfy his readers and to not expect infallibility [2 Macc 2:19-23; 15:37-39]. That’s why these books were rejected by the Jews who were in charge of the OT canon [Rom 3:2], even though they actually believe the Maccabean revolt as a real historical event). During the intertestamental period, the Seleuci (Greek) emperor Antiochus IV, who arrogantly gave himself the title Epiphanes (“God Manifest”), launched a brutal campaign to stamp out the Jewish religion and force hellenization (Greek culture) upon Judea. An altar to Zeus was erected inside the Jewish temple (pagan idol placed in God’s house). Swine was sacrificed on the Holy Altar (desecration by an unclean animal), and the Temple plundered (the sanctuary was left completely empty). According to 1 Maccabees 1:54, on the 15th day of the Hebrew month Kislev in 167BC, Antiochus’ forces erected the “ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION” upon the altar: a pagan altar dedicated to the Greek god Zeus Olympius, featuring a literal statue or image of Zeus carved to resemble Antiochus himself. To compound this horror, Antiochus ordered pigs (the ultimate ceremonially unclean animal under Levitical Law) to be sacrificed on God’s holy altar and had the pig broth splattered across the sacred rooms of the Temple, rendering it completely un-worshippable and “desolate” from three years until the Maccabean Revolt successfully recaptured and cleansed the sanctuary (celebrated as Hanukkah). Going back to telescoping and dual fulfillment: (1) The First Peak (The 70AD Siege): When Jesus speaks in Mt 24, he is telling his disciples that a second, greater “abomination of desolation” is coming to the Temple. To understand exactly what this looked like in the first century, we must compare Matthew’s account with the parallel passage in Luke 21:20: "And when ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies, then know that the desolation thereof is nigh" (KJV). Luke, writing primarily to a Gentile audience who might not understand deep Hebrew idioms like “abomination of desolation,” translates the meaning plainly: The abomination is the pagan Roman army surrounding the holy city. The Roman legions carried military standards or banners called signa and aquilae (eagles). These were not mere flags; they were literal idols. The Romans engraved images of their gods and the deified Roman Emperor directly onto these metal poles, and the soldiers regularly offered pagan sacrifices and worship to these military ensigns. The fulfillment occurred in 70AD, when the Roman armies under Titus broke through the walls. Jewish historian Josephus records that after setting the Temple on fire, the Roman soldiers brought their idolatrous standards directly into the sacred Temple courts, planted them opposite the eastern gate, and offered pagan sacrifices to them right on the holy ground. Because the early Christians listened to Jesus’ warning in Mt 24:15, the moment they saw the initial approach of the Roman legions under Cestius Gallus surrounding the city in 66AD, they recognized the “abomination of desolation.” When the Roman army inexplicably withdrew for a brief window, the Christians took that opportunity to flee Jerusalem, escaping across the Jordan River to the mountain city of Pella, completely sparing their lives from the horrific slaughter that followed. (2) The Taller Second Peak (End-Times): Just as Antiochus Epiphanes IV was a historical shadow of the Roman destruction in 70AD, both of these events serve as a prophetic blueprint for the ultimate, global Abomination of Desolation at the end of human history. Paul references this future, global fulfillment in 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4, describing the final Antichrist: "...that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition; Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God" (KJV). In the final crisis of human history, the pattern will repeat one last time on a global stage. A blasphemous, deceptive political leader (the Antichrist) will establish a covenant, break it, and set up an ultimate system of idolatrous, mandatory worship inside a holy place(most likely when the Third Jewish Temple gets built), demanding that the world worship his image rather than the true living God. Just as it did in the days of Antiochus and in 70AD, this final act of spiritual treason will trigger the climactic, swift, and final wrath of God at the physical Second Coming of Jesus Christ.

16.x: Once the visual cue of the “abomination of desolation” appears in v.15, Jesus shifts from general warnings to highly specific, life-or-death survival tactics. The language in this section highlights absolute urgency, showing that when the trap snaps shut on Jerusalem, a delay of even a few seconds will mean physical death. “Then let them which be in Judea..”: Jesus localizes the immediate geography. He is giving directives specifically to the first-century church living in the Roman province of Judea. “..flee into the mountains”: They are told not to fortify the city or stay behind its stone walls to fight. Jerusalem was a trap. They were to escape to the rugged, cavernous mountain across the Jordan River. Historically, when the Roman general Cestius Gallus inexplicably lifted his initial siege in 66AD, the Christian community recognized the window of opportunity and fled to the mountain city of Pella in the Decapolis, completely escaping the horrific slaughter of 70AD.

17.x: “..him which is on the housetop..”: First-century Middle Eastern homes had flat roofs used as additional living spaces for relaxing, praying, or drying crops. “..not come down to take anything..”: The external staircases on these homes allowed someone to descend directly to the street without entering the house. Jesus says: “Don’t go inside to pack a bag. Don’t grab your money, your legal documents, or your family heirlooms. The microsecond you see the sign, run down the outer stairs and out of the city immediately.”

18.x: “..neither let him which is in the field return back..”: A laborer or farmer working in the fields outside the city walls would typically strip down to a simple tunic for heavy manual labor, leaving his heavy outer cloak (“clothes”) at home or at the edge of the plot. “..to take his clothes”: Jesus warns them not to go back for their jacket or wrap. Survival matters more than comfort. The emphasis is entirely on an instantaneous, unhindered exit.

19.x: “And woe unto them..”: This is an expression of profound pastoral sorrow and pity, not a condemnation. “..that are with child, and to them that give suck..”: Pregnant women and mothers nursing infant children (“give suck”) will face agonizing physical limitations. A brutal, rapid foot-flight across rugged mountainous terrain is naturally slower and far more punishing for a mother shielding a newborn or carrying a child.

20.x: “..not in the winter..”: Winter in Judea brought freezing rains, bitter cold, and swollen, raging rivers (like the Jordan) that were nearly impossible to cross on foot. “..neither on the sabbath day”: on the Sabbath, the Jewish authorities locked the heavy gates of Jerusalem, which would trap anyone inside the city walls. There was also social stigma related to the Sabbath. Traveling a long distance on the Sabbath violated traditional Jewish law. Anyone fleeing on that day would instantly draw suspicion, or face physical resistance from religious zealots monitoring the roads.

21.x: “For then shall be great tribulation..”: The word tribulation is “thlipsis,” meaning crushing pressure, oppression, or affliction. “..such as was not since the beginning of the world..”: telescoping again: (1) First Peak (70AD): For the Jewish nation, the siege of 70AD was an unparalleled, apocalyptic horror. Jewish historian Josephus records that 1.1 million Jews were slaughtered or died of starvation inside the city, 97,000 were sold into brutal Roman slavery, and the starvation became so severe that mothers resorted to CANNIBALIZING their own infants to survive. It was the absolute, catastrophic end of the Old Covenant temple age. (Col 1:16 KJV). A created archangel cannot be the Creator of all angelic beings.

The full text reads: “Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Phil 2:5-11 KJV). Phil 2:5-11 from a Oneness perspective: (Verse 5): “Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus”: since the mind in you, is the same also in Christ Jesus, here it is referring to the HUMAN mind of Christ Jesus, not the eternal divine Spirit that is God. The focus is not on the transcendent nature of God, which we humans cannot duplicate, but on the attitude and conduct of the man Jesus, which we can imitate. (Verse 6): “Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God”: there are two forms: (1) the form of God (a divine Spirit), that only God can have (Isa 43:10;45:5), & (2) the form of a servant (a human), that we all have. Jesus is “in the form of God” because God-in-the-flesh is STILL the same as God-before-the-flesh. The man Jesus had access to the divine Spirit “without limit” (Jn 3:34 BSB) (the same as God), but while on Earth, he decided to not use his divine prerogatives (“thought it not robbery to be equal with God”). The word “equal” comes from the Greek “isos”, and it means: “equal” or “the same.” For example: “God gave them the SAME(isos) gift..” (Acts 17:11 BSB). So essentially what v.6 is saying is: “even though the man Jesus was still God, he did not consider being the same as God(omniscient, omnipresent, omnipotent) something to be used to his own advantage” (v.6); this is very close to how the NIV actually translated it: “Who, being in the very nature God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage” (v.6 NIV). The use of “equal” does not require Jesus to be a secondary divine person. If it did, the Bible would have a contradiction, for God has no equal and there is none like Him (Isa 46:5,9). If “equal with” indicates a distinct divine person, then Jesus would not merely be a distinct person from the Father, but a distinct person from “God” altogether. So here, what we see is the distinction between the human and the divine Spirit: although the human born of Mary possessed the nature & identity of God by: (1) being Immanuel - “God with us” (Mt 1:23); (2) being the “express image of His person(hypostasis)” (Heb 1:3): notice there is only one invisible divine hypostasis(person), of whom the man Jesus is the image of (he is not a second divine person, but the visible image of the one divine person); (3) being a man “FULL of the Holy Spirit(God)” (Lk 4:1): “For in him dwelleth ALL the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9) & (4) having access to this divine Spirit “without limit” (Jn 3:34 BSB); yet, he humbled himself & willingly gave up his divine prerogatives & privileges by accepting his human limitations. Since the Father (the divine Spirit) had given EVERYTHING to the human Son (“All things are delivered unto me of my Father..”, Mt 11:27 KJV), at any moment, the man Jesus could have used His divine glory, as in the transfiguration, but instead he veiled his glory, the Father’s glory (Jn 8:54 BSB), and displayed the ordinary human appearance as the Son of Man. (Verse 7): “But made himself of no reputation(‘emptied himself’ BSB), and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men”: Trinitarians see this “emptying” as pre-incarnate God-the-Son giving up all his divine attributes to become a man totally dependent on the Father. Rather, this “emptying” occurred when the human, as the suffering servant, “poured out his soul unto death” (Isa 53:12 KJV). His “emptying” includes his entire human ministry. The human humbled himself, laid aside any divine privileges(his unlimited access to the Spirit of the Father) and accepted his mission of being birthed in Mary’s womb and sent out into the world as a suffering servant(“taking upon the form of a servant”) under his human limitations (“in the likeness of men”). The man Jesus always knew his purpose since he was a kid. At 12 years old, he was already saying things like: “Didn’t you know I had to be in my Father’s house?” (Lk 2:49 KJV) - fully aware of his earthly mission. The name of “Jesus” is the ONLY name given to men under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:10,12). It’s the name prophesied about: “And the Lord shall be king over all the earth: in that day shall there be ONE Lord, and HIS NAME ONE” (Zech 14:9 KJV). When Mary was overshadowed by the Holy Spirit (baby Jesus’ Father), Mary was specifically instructed to name the baby “Jesus” because “he shall save his people from their sins” (Mt 1:21 KJV). His name literally means what he was going to do: “YHWH-saves” us from our sins. The human born of Mary INHERITED (“he hath by inheritance obtained a more excellent name,” Heb 1:4 KJV) the name of the Father. The word “inherited” means that the name belonged to the Father before being passed down to him. That’s why Jesus could say: “Holy FATHER, protect them BY YOUR NAME, THE NAME YOU GAVE ME” (Jn 17:11 BSB). This is also why Jesus said in Mt 28:18 that ALL AUTHORITY had been given unto him (from the divine spirit to the human), therefore go and baptize in the name of other divine people…. Of course not! Now if any man have not the SPIRIT OF CHRIST, he is none of his” (Rom 8:9 KJV), because “the Lord(Jesus) is that Spirit” (2 Cor 3:17). (Verse 10): “That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth;”: to confirm everything explained above, the name given to the Son is “Jesus”, not “Lord” (as Trinitarians try to teach). Here it says that every knee will bow to the name of Jesus, yet in the OT YHWH says: “there is no God else beside me(YHWH); a just God and a Saviour; there is none beside me(YHWH). Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else. That unto me(YHWH) EVERY KNEE SHALL BOW, every tongue shall swear” (Isa 45:21-23 KJV) - notice the speaker is YHWH, who says “I am God, and there is none else.” He swears by Himself because there is no greater authority (“God made promises… because He could swear by no greater, He sware by Himself” Heb 6:13 KJV). Yet the prophecy is fulfilled in Jesus because Jesus is the same YHWH of the OT in the flesh. (Verse 11): “And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.”: Calling Jesus “Lord” could mean two things: (1) that Jesus, as God in the flesh, is the sovereign master and owner of everything; and (2) Trinitarians like to read “Lord” as “YHWH”. The Greek Septuagint (LXX) translated “YHWH” as “Lord” in order to respect the divine name and prevent taking it in vain. So here you would see two YHWH’s: Jesus who is Lord(YHWH), and God the Father who is YHWH as well. Two distinct divine persons sharing the divine essence of God (YHWH). However, this interpretation would contradict the OT, which explicitly states that YHWH is one, not two nor three: “The LORD our God is one LORD(YHWH)” (Deut 6:4 KJV); “the LORD(YHWH) He is God; there is none else beside Him” (Deut 4:35 KJV); “O LORD(YHWH) God: for there is none like thee, neither is there any God beside thee” (2 Sam 7:22 KJV); “I the LORD(YHWH), the first, and with the last; I am HE(not they)” (Isa 41:4 KJV); “I am the first, and I am the last; and beside me there is no God” (Isa 44:6 KJV); “Before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me. I, even I, am the LORD(YHWH); and beside me there is no saviour” (Isa 43:10-11 KJV); etc etc. YHWH clearly says He is one, yet Trinitarians will take this “one” to mean a “unity of divine persons.” As support, they will use verses that sound like there are two YHWHs. For example: “Then the LORD(YHWH) rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD(YHWH) out of heaven” (Gen 19:24 KJV). However, this conclusion lacks information. First, Jesus cites Deut 6:4 in Mk 12:29, and when he says “the LORD is ONE(heis),” he uses the Greek word for SINGULAR MASCULINE ONE that demands one person, that is why the Amplified Bible explicitly adds “one person” in Gal 3:20: “God is [only] one(heis) Person” (AMPC). 37.x: “But as the days of Noe[Noah] were..”: Jesus explicitly picks a historic, global catastrophe as the direct type and shadow for his physical return. He does not compare his coming to an era of global revival or widespread political peace, but to an era marked by profound spiritual apathy, wickedness, and sudden judgement. “...so shall also the coming of the Son of man be”: The structural pattern of Noah’s flood (long warning, absolute indifference by the masses, sudden supernatural judgement, and immediate separation) is the exact blueprint for “the coming”(Parousia).

38.x: “..eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage..”: Notice what Jesus lists here. He does not highlight monstrous crimes like murder or idolatry (though Gen 6:5 notes those were present); he highlights normal, legitimate, everyday human routines. The deadly sin of Noah’s generation was not merely gross wickedness; it was complete spiritual blindness caused by earthly absorption. They were so consumed with living, social maneuvering, business, and pleasure that they completely ignored the giant wooden ark being built in their face. They lived as if tomorrow would always look like today.

39.x: “And knew not..”: It was not that they hadn’t been warned, as Noah was a “preacher of righteousness” for decades (2 Peter 2:5). They “knew not” because they voluntarily refused to believe. They mistook God’s long-suffering patience for approval or non-existence. “..until the flood came, and took them all away..”: When the rain started, the door of the ark was already sealed by God Himself (Gen 7:16). There was no second chance, no extended discussion, and no late entry. The judgement was total and immediate. “..so shall also the coming of the Son of man be”: Just like the floodgate snapped shut, the final arrival of Christ will cut human history in two with absolute finality.

40.x: “Then shall two be in the field..”: Jesus shifts to a workplace setting: two men performing the same heavy, outdoor manual labor side-by-side. “..the one shall be taken, and the other left”: On the surface, both men look identical. They wear the same clothes, work the same dirt, and earn the same wage. But spiritually, one belongs to the Kingdom of God, and the other is anchored to the earth. A sudden, supernatural divide occurs in a microsecond. The “taken” could mean two things: (1) In verse 39, the flood came and “took them [the wicked] all away.” Following the exact grammar of Noah’s analogy, the ones who are “taken” are swept away in divine judgement, while the ones “left” remain safe in the kingdom of earth (the ark). (2) The Greek word for “taken” (paralambano) literally means “to take alongside to oneself with affection”, and this is the exact word that Jesus uses in John 14:3 (“I will come again, and receive[paralambano] you unto myself”). In this light, the elect are supernaturally “taken” by the angels to meet the Lord, while the wicked are “left” behind for destruction. In either interpretation, the core truth is unshakeable: The coming of Christ brings an instantaneous, irreversible separation between the saved and the lost.

41.x: “Two women shall be grinding at the mill…”: This describes domestic, home-based labor. In ancient Judea, two women sat facing each other, turning a heavy circular stone to grind grain for the morning bread. “..one shall be taken, and the other left”: Neither close family ties, shared domestic responsibilities, nor physical proximity can save a person. Salvation is intensely individual. You cannot enter the kingdom on the coattails of a godly spouse, parent, or coworker.

42.x: “Watch therefore..”: This is the imperative climax of the entire chapter. The Greek word is “gregoreite,” meaning to stay awake, remain alert, and maintain constant spiritual vigilance. “..for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come”: Because the date cannot be calculated by charts or calendar predictions, readiness cannot be delayed to “later.” Readiness must be a continuous, present-tense state of being.

Many people treat salvation like an insurance policy they can secure at the last minute. But Jesus warns that his coming will occur on an ordinary, unannounced day, while people are plowing fields, grinding flour, making plans, and living in mundane routine. Spiritual alertness (“Watch therefore”) requires three active realities: (1) Spiritual Sobriety: Refusing to let the legitimate cares, pleasures, and routines of this world dull out hunger for God (Lk 21:34). (2) Continuous Obedience: Walking firmly in the Apostolic blueprint of Acts 2:38, living a consecrated, holy life daily so that whenever the trumpet sounds, our lamps are trimmed and burning. (3) Expectant Waiting: Living with the daily awareness that Jesus could break through the clouds at any moment.

43.x: “But know this..” Jesus commands focused mental engagement. He uses an everyday illustration of home security to expose human inconsistency. “..if the goodman of the house had known in what watch…”: The “goodman” refers to the master or head of the household. In the ancient world, the night was divided into four distinct guard shifts (“watches”). “..the thief would come, he would have watched..”: A homeowner who receives advance notice of a burglary does not go to sleep; he stays alert during that specific hour. “...and would not have suffered his house to be broken up”: Ancient homes were often made of sun-dried mud brick, allowing a thief to literally dig or break through (diorysso) the wall unnoticed under the cover of darkness. The lesson is sharp: people exercise extreme diligence to protect physical possessions, yet often treat their eternal souls with total carelessness.

44.x: “Therefore be ye also ready..”: Notice the imperative. Readiness is not a passive emotion; it is an active, ongoing state of spiritual preparation. “..for in such an hour as ye think not..”: Like a thief, no one knows the hour of the Lord’s return, but a believer must be ready at all times: both, in case he comes sooner than expected (vv.43-51), or in case he comes after than expected (Mt 25:1-13).

45.x: The primary duty assigned to the “faithful and wise servant” is to feed the master’s household with proper nourishment at the proper time. This highlights the responsibility of ministers and leaders to consistently proclaim the uncompromised Word of God, dispensing truth that sustains the Church.

46.x: “Blessed is that servant..”: The beatitude is pronounced not on the servant who started well, but on the one who finishes well. “..shall find so doing”: Christianity is not a religion of past achievements; it is a life of present consistency. The Lord rewards active duty, not idle memory.

47.x: “...he shall make him ruler over all his goods”: Temporary faithfulness in managing God’s earthly household yields eternal authority and stewardship in the Kingdom to come: “Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities” (Lk 19:17 KJV).

48.x: “But and if that evil servant shall say in his heart..”: Apostasy rarely begins with an immediate public renunciation of faith; it begins as a quiet, internal shift in the heart (“shall say in his heart”). “My lord delayeth his coming..”: This is the root toxin of spiritual backsliding. The moment a person stops expecting Christ’s imminent return, their lifestyle begins to decompose. Presuming upon time leads directly to carnal indulgence(sexual immortality, drugs, mistreatment of others, etc).

49.x: “And shall begin to smite his fellowservants..”: Once the fear of the Lord and the expectancy of his return vanish, internal abuse sets in. This manifests as spiritual tyranny, harshness, biting words, and division among believers. “...and to eat and drink with the drunken”: The evil servant lowers his standards and joins hands with the world. He abandons consecration, holiness, and sobriety, fully indulging in worldly pleasures and compromise.

50.x: “The lord of that servant shall come..”: The delay was an illusion. The master’s return is fixed, sovereign, and inescapable. “...when he looketh not for him..”: Judgement strikes at the peak of the servant’s self-indulgence and false security.

51.x: “And shall cut him asunder..”: The Greek word for “asunder” is “dichotomeo,” literally meaning “to cut into two pieces.” It represents the severe execution of divine justice for hypocrisy and treason. “...appoint him his portion with the hypocrites..”: The servant’s ultimate tragedy is that despite wearing the uniform of the master’s household, his heart belonged to the wicked. He is assigned to the exact place reserved for pretenders. “..there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth”: A description of absolute despair, conscious torment, and eternal regret over wasted opportunity.
